newsitem.title: UK: New test shows whether cancer drugs are working.
newsitem.headline: New test shows whether cancer drugs are working.

text.p: British cancer researchers said on Monday they had developed a new test that showed whether cancer drugs were working on a tumour.
The test shows within 24 hours whether chemotherapy is killing the tumour, giving doctors a chance to try another drug quickly if the first one is not.
"It's a very rapid means of determining whether the drugs are working," said Mitch Dowsett of the Institute of Cancer Research, who worked on the study.

Dowsett, whose team works at the Royal Marsden Hospital, told the Institute's annual meeting the test showed that giving drugs to women with breast cancer before they had surgery helped start a process called apoptosis, or programmed cell death.
Cells are supposed to die when they are damaged, and failure of this apoptosis process can cause tumours to grow.
"First it confirms that in solid tumours in humans that apoptosis is indeed induced by cytotoxic drugs," Dowsett said in an interview before the meeting.

"Second, it potentially gives us a predictive test for individual patients -- does that patient have a responsive tumour to that particular treatment, and if she doesn't, she has a better chance of moving on to a better treatment."

Dowsett said previous tests had been clumsy and time-consuming. "What we have been doing until now has been taking a sliver of tissue -- a Tru-cut biopsy -- and then physically counting cells under a microscope. It's a more invasive procedure that involves using local anaesthetic."

The new method involves using a syringe similar to those used to take blood. "We can get tens of thousands, up to millions of cells off tumours," Dowsett said. These could be counted in an instrument called a flow cytometer, which counted them in minutes as compared to hours under a microscope.
"This is such a simple observation, but no one's done it in the past," Dowsett said.
The team's work is also described in a letter to this week's Lancet medical journal.
